analysis.one_liner: Creates a universal child care and early learning program with fees capped at 7% of family income.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or any vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an entitlement: every child not yet old enough for school could enroll in a federally supported child care and early learning program, regardless of income, disability, citizenship, or whether a parent works. Families below 200% of the poverty line would pay nothing, and no family would pay more than 7% of its income no matter how many children it enrolls. The federal government would pay at least 90% of the cost, delivered through states, cities, tribal organizations, and nonprofits, with requirements that the child care workforce be paid fairly and bargain collectively.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children gain the most: free or sharply capped child care would replace some of the most expensive line items in a household budget, and the guarantee is universal, covering children regardless of income or parents' employment status. Child care workers gain wage, benefit, and bargaining standards, and existing providers gain a large new funding stream. Parents of children with disabilities, homeless children, children in foster care, and dual language learners get priority access and tailored services.

how_it_helps.text: Every covered child is entitled to enroll in a child care and early learning program, with an uncapped entitlement that cannot be limited by funding caps [S3].
Families below 200% of the poverty line pay no fee, and fees for everyone else are capped at 7% of family income no matter how many children they enroll [S2].
The federal share of program costs is at least 90%, and 100% for children of migrant and seasonal farmworkers and for Native American children [S3].
The bill requires sponsors to support fair compensation for child care teachers and staff and directs sponsors to recognize and bargain with unions representing providers and center staff [S3].
Children participate regardless of family income, disability status, citizenship status, or employment of a family member [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through appropriations of 'such sums as may be necessary' — the bill writes itself as an open-ended, uncapped entitlement rather than a fixed annual budget. States and localities must also maintain their existing child care spending (a maintenance-of-effort rule) and cover up to 10% of costs. The wealthiest households, as the largest federal taxpayers, would bear the largest share of the financing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers through an open-ended entitlement

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' with an uncapped entitlement, meaning Congress would commit to whatever the program costs each year without a fixed budget [S3].

National program standards and compensation requirements would impose new compliance and wage costs on child care providers, which could push some small home-based providers out of the program or raise operating costs [S3].

A federal entitlement delivered through sponsors could compete with or disrupt existing child care arrangements, and states would be barred from reducing their own child care spending to offset the new federal money [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to families with young children is large and direct: child care is among the biggest expenses working households face, and the bill converts it into a fee capped at 7% of income, free for lower-income families. The honest cost is fiscal: an uncapped federal entitlement of this scope is expensive and would be one of the largest new commitments in the federal budget, and the wage and quality mandates could strain smaller providers. Whether the trade is worth it depends on weighing a major new permanent program against one of the clearest, broadest household cost burdens — but the bill never got far enough for that debate to happen in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP committee on February 9, 2023, and the committee took no action on it for the rest of the Congress, so it never reached the Senate floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced S. 388 in the Senate on February 9, 2023, joined by nine Democratic senators and one Independent as cosponsors [S1].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's record — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].
All ten cosponsors were Democrats or Independents; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Existing child care providers avoided new federal standards, wage requirements, and public competition, and taxpayers avoided a large new uncapped entitlement — while families with young children gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing providers and the status quo

sides.party_line_note: All ten cosponsors were Democrats or Independents and no Republican supported the bill; with a Senate in which neither party had the 60 votes typically needed to advance contentious legislation, a bill with no Republican support never advanced past committee.

industries.industry: Child care and early learning providers (centers and home-based)
industries.note: The bill would make public funding flow through states, localities, tribal organizations, and nonprofits to providers of every kind, including for-profit delegate agencies, giving the sector a permanent, uncapped revenue channel. Providers would gain guaranteed federal payments while being held to national quality and wage standards.

industries.industry: Child care workers and family child care providers
industries.note: The bill requires compensation that meets federal standards and directs sponsors to recognize and bargain with unions representing teachers, staff, and home-based providers. The workforce, which is overwhelmingly low-paid, would be the direct beneficiary of the wage provisions.

An uncapped federal entitlement of this size would be financed by general federal revenue, so the largest taxpayers and employers would bear the cost. Employers would also benefit indirectly from a larger, more stable labor supply as child care becomes affordable.
